Devin bots own the goal

17 November 2026 · Reading time: 3 minutes · Audio in the app: 4 minutes. Listening to the briefing is part of Sapaude Premium.

Cognition has launched Devin Bots, persistent agents that take on a goal instead of a single task and lead several Devin coding agents to reach it.

Sapaude retells the story in its own words. The source is below. Publisher: Sapaude.

In three points

Three points, in this order: what the source shows, where that claim stops, and what to check next.

  1. Cognition says a Bot has its own memory and tools, investigates, delegates work to Devins, checks the results and decides what to do next, coming back only for decisions that need a person.
  2. Its main example: an Android Bot built Devin's Android app in 44 days, with 1,134 merged pull requests and 183 messages from the engineer who set it up. The figures are Cognition's own.
  3. Engineers still define what success means, how the Bot checks its work and what it may change without approval. Devin Bots are available now at devin.ai/bots; the post gives no price.

From tasks to outcomes

Cognition introduced Devin Bots on November 17, 2026. The company calls them "engineering teammates that own your goals and lead teams of Devins to deliver them."

The starting point is a familiar gap. A coding agent can finish every task it is given and still leave the engineer responsible for moving the project forward: spotting the next problem, investigating fixes, checking whether a change helped. A Bot is meant to take on more of that. Cognition describes it as a persistent agent with its own memory and tools that can lead multiple Devins in parallel. It investigates, delegates, evaluates the results, keeps context across sessions and brings back only the decisions that need human judgment.

An Android app in 44 days

The headline example is internal. Devin had an iOS app and no Android engineers. On September 28, engineer Samyok created an "Android Bot" and told it to product-manage the Android app, starting with what was blocking it. According to Cognition, the Bot filed tickets, started a Devin session for each one and merged the pull requests that passed CI and Devin Review.

After 44 days the company counts 1,134 merged pull requests, 344,651 lines of Kotlin, 2,841 screenshot tests and 1,217 closed tickets. Samyok sent 183 messages, mostly about decisions such as a PR that needed a security review. The app is now in open testing on Google Play.

A second Bot runs a layout check on the web app every three hours. Cognition says it contributed 159 merged pull requests in three weeks and cut lag by 70 percent. A third setup runs a small game studio with about 20 Bots, which went from about 50 to 1,900 pull requests a week.

A responsibility instead of a ticket

Cognition frames the change as a difference in wording. "Port this feature to Android" is a task. "Keep Android at parity with iOS" is a responsibility: it names the outcome and leaves the path to the Bot. Because a Bot watches everything that affects its goal, the company argues, it can find work nobody would have assigned.

Decisions that need input land in a "Needs You" inbox. Bots report through Slack, iMessage or the Devin app, and several Bots can coordinate with each other.

What engineers still decide

The post is clear that the groundwork stays with people. Engineers define what success means for a scope, build the tests and metrics the Bot uses to judge its work, and set how independently it may act: which systems it can reach, what it can change, and when spending or releases need approval.

All figures come from Cognition and its own teams. Pull request counts say little about code quality or review effort, and there is no independent test yet. Devin Bots are available at devin.ai/bots; the post does not mention pricing.

What you can do

The shift Cognition describes is in the assignment: "Keep Android at parity with iOS" instead of "Port this feature to Android." Whether that holds up outside Cognition's own teams has not been shown yet.
